person.name: Erich_Kästner
person.summary: Emil Erich Kästner was a German writer, poet, screenwriter, and satirist, best known for his witty, socially observant poems and for children’s classics such as Emil and the Detectives, Lisa and Lottie, and The Flying Classroom. A key figure of Weimar-era Neue Sachlichkeit, he remained in Germany under National Socialism, where his books were banned and burned while he continued to publish some works abroad and write screenplays under a pseudonym. After 1945 he settled in Munich, working as editor, cabaret writer, radio author, and children’s author, and received the Hans Christian Andersen Award in 1960 for his autobiography When I Was a Little Boy.

events.title: Birth in Dresden
events.description: Emil Erich Kästner was born in Dresden, Saxony, the only child of master saddlemaker Emil Richard Kästner and his wife Ida Amalia (née Augustin). He grew up on Königsbrücker Straße in the Äußere Neustadt district, an urban environment that later featured prominently and nostalgically in his autobiographical writing.

images.caption: Birth house of Erich Kästner in Dresden’s Äußere Neustadt district.

events.title: Attends teacher training school
events.description: Kästner entered a teacher training school in Dresden, beginning professional preparation for a career as a state-school teacher. He remained there until 1916, when he dropped out shortly before taking the qualifying exams, an early break with the conventional career path expected for a lower-middle-class son.

events.title: Drafted into Saxon Army
events.description: During the First World War Kästner was drafted into the Royal Saxon Army and trained with a heavy artillery unit in Dresden. Although never sent to the front, he experienced brutal military drilling that contributed to a lifelong heart condition and profoundly shaped the antimilitarism that pervades his later writings.

images.caption: Flag of Germany, representing the country whose army Kästner was drafted into during World War I.

events.date_note: The article states 'In the autumn of 1919' for his enrollment; month approximated as September
events.title: Begins studies in Leipzig
events.description: In the autumn of 1919 Kästner enrolled at the University of Leipzig to study history, philosophy, German studies, and theater. Over the following years his studies also took him to Rostock and Berlin, laying the academic and intellectual foundations for his later work as a critic, satirist, and author.

images.caption: Erich Kästner School in Leipzig-Gohlis, named in honor of the author’s later legacy in the city where he studied.

events.title: Works for Neue Leipziger Zeitung
events.description: While completing his university studies, Kästner supported himself as a journalist and critic for the Neue Leipziger Zeitung. Between 1923 and 1927 he wrote reviews and articles that began to establish his reputation for sharp, socially observant criticism, though his increasingly critical tone and the publication of an erotic poem later led to his dismissal.

events.title: Receives doctoral degree
events.description: Kästner was awarded a doctorate from the University of Leipzig for his thesis on Frederick the Great and German literature. The degree marked the culmination of his formal academic training and reinforced his authority as a literary scholar and critic in the cultural life of the Weimar Republic.

events.title: Moves to Berlin
events.description: After being dismissed from the Neue Leipziger Zeitung in 1927 for his critical reviews and the publication of the erotic poem "Abendlied des Kammervirtuosen", Kästner moved to Berlin. He continued to write for the paper under the pseudonym "Berthold Bürger" and soon became a prolific contributor to major Berlin newspapers and magazines, integrating himself into the vibrant literary culture of the capital.

events.date_note: The article notes 'In the autumn of 1928' for the publication of Emil und die Detektive; month approximated as October
events.title: Releases Emil and the Detectives
events.description: In the autumn of 1928 Kästner published his best-known children’s book, "Emil und die Detektive", illustrated by Walter Trier. Set in contemporary Berlin rather than a fairy-tale world and largely free of overt moralizing, the novel was a sensation, selling around two million copies in Germany and eventually being translated into dozens of languages, shaping the genre of child-detective fiction.

images.caption: Title page of a 1931 edition of Erich Kästner’s children’s novel "Emil und die Detektive".

events.title: Publishes first poetry book
events.description: Kästner’s first book of poems, "Herz auf Taille", was published in 1928. Its clear, ironic, and socially observant style exemplified the Neue Sachlichkeit movement and helped establish him as a leading figure in contemporary German poetry, known for "Gebrauchslyrik"—lyrics for everyday use.

images.caption: Dust jacket designed by Erich Ohser for Kästner’s 1932 poetry volume "Gesang zwischen den Stühlen", reflecting his publishing success in poetry.

events.title: Publishes Fabian novel
events.description: Kästner’s only major novel for adults, "Fabian: Die Geschichte eines Moralisten" (Fabian: The Story of a Moralist), appeared in 1931. The book follows an unemployed literary scholar through the rapid social and moral decline of late Weimar Berlin, using cinematic techniques such as rapid cuts and montage to portray the upheavals of the time.

events.title: Books burned in Berlin
events.description: On 10 May 1933, after the Nazi seizure of power, Kästner’s works were publicly burned in Berlin as "contrary to the German spirit" during regime-orchestrated book burnings. Kästner, who had chosen not to go into exile, witnessed the event in person and was repeatedly interrogated by the Gestapo, later writing about the experience and its impact on his stance as an internal critic of the regime.

events.title: Writes Münchhausen screenplay
events.description: In 1942 Kästner received a special exemption under the Nazi regime to write the screenplay for the Ufa prestige film "Münchhausen", celebrating the studio’s twenty-fifth anniversary. Working under the pseudonym "Berthold Bürger", he crafted a fantastical script that allowed him to continue writing for cinema despite being officially excluded from the Reich writers’ organization.

events.date_note: He was in Mayrhofen when the war ended in 1945; month approximated as May to reflect Germany’s surrender
events.title: Ends war in Mayrhofen
events.description: In the final months of the Second World War, Kästner and others traveled to Mayrhofen in Tyrol under the pretense of scouting locations for a non-existent film, "Das falsche Gesicht", to escape the looming Soviet assault on Berlin and threats from the SS. He was in Mayrhofen when the war ended and later documented this period in his diary, published as "Notabene 45" and, in a more complete version, as "Das Blaue Buch".

events.title: Wins Hans Christian Andersen Award
events.description: In 1960 Kästner received the international Hans Christian Andersen Award for writing, the highest recognition for a children’s author, honoring his overall contribution to children’s literature and specifically his autobiographical work "Als ich ein kleiner Junge war" (When I Was a Little Boy). The award confirmed his standing as one of the leading children’s writers of the twentieth century.

events.title: Death in Munich
events.description: Erich Kästner died in Munich on 29 July 1974 at the age of 75, after years of declining health and increasing alcoholism. He was buried in the Bogenhauser Friedhof in Munich, closing a life that spanned Imperial Germany, the Weimar Republic, National Socialism, and the Federal Republic.

images.caption: Grave of Erich Kästner and his companion Luiselotte Enderle at the Bogenhauser Friedhof in Munich.
